annotations.text:
WORTH TELLING -- what this is

You send from the desk. One picture per customer per fortnight. Site stage goes on the record. Everything on this canvas follows from those three.

THE ALGORITHM IS FIVE RULES, AND THE RAIL SHOWS THEM. There is no model. At forty-five customers a trained model has nothing to learn from and cannot say why it picked anything; five rules read off your own invoices, stock book and follow-ups are more accurate AND every row can explain itself -- which matters, because you are the one pressing send.

A CUSTOMER IS ON THE LIST ONLY IF ONE OF SIX THINGS IS TRUE ABOUT THEM:
1. DUE BY RHYTHM -- they buy a line every N days, at least three times, and the next is within 3 days.
2. THEY ASKED -- a follow-up or sourcing ask, and it has come in. Highest priority: it is a recommendation they requested.
3. PRICE DOWN FOR THEM -- what they buy now costs at least 5% less than THEY last paid.
4. SITE STAGE -- their build moved to a stage they have not bought for yet. Sized from their last order.
5. COME BACK -- one order, then silence past 21 days.
6. GOES WITH -- never the reason on its own; it is the third frame, and it comes from What goes with what.

ONE REASON PER CUSTOMER, THE DEAREST. The runners-up are listed in the open row and wait a fortnight -- and if the customer buys the thing anyway, the reason stops being true and goes.

HELD BACK, AND NAMED. Told inside 14 days, chased inside 7, past terms, no phone number. Somebody you are chasing for money does not also get a picture of cement.

NOTHING SENDS ITSELF. Share opens WhatsApp with the GIF attached and the customer's chat chosen; you press send. The app writes it down as told when you do, and the fortnight starts from then.

DID IT WORK is bought-within-14-days of being told, per reason. Not proof -- Kato would have bought cement anyway -- but it is what the books can say, and reasons that never convert sink on their own.

SITE STAGE -- the input you agreed to add

One dropdown and a date on the customer form. Seven values: Not a site (a retailer), Foundation, Walling, Roofing, Plumbing & electrical, Finishing, Done.

WHY IT PREDICTS BEST: a build goes in an order, and each stage buys a different shelf. A rhythm can only say "more of the same"; a stage says what comes NEXT, before they have bought any of it. That is the one thing no figure in the books can do.

WHAT EACH STAGE BUYS is read from your own invoices where the stage was known at the time, and from the list on the form until there are enough of them -- and the screen says which it used.

IT GOES STALE BY ITSELF. The date is what makes it safe: a stage older than 60 days stops counting until it is confirmed, so a site that finished in July does not get roofing sheets in September. The rail lists who to ask.

NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. WHAT "REPLY YES" COMMITS YOU TO. I have drawn "we keep it for you" -- which means when they reply, YOU create the order and set the goods aside. Nothing is reserved automatically. If that is a promise you would rather not make in writing, the frame becomes "REPLY YES" and "WE WILL CALL YOU", which is one line.

2. "SAME PRICE" WHERE THE LAST PRICE IS OLD. The rule I drew: show the CURRENT price always, and add the stamp only where it is unchanged since they last paid. For somebody who last bought a year ago that stamp is technically true and practically strange -- I would cap it at 90 days. Say the word.

3. THE 14-DAY MEASURE. Bought within 14 days counts as a win. Too short and a fortnightly buyer never counts; too long and everything counts.

4. WHO SETS A SITE STAGE. Drawn desk-only, as you said for sending. But the field is where the answer is, and an agent standing on the site knows it. Lower stakes than sending -- worth reconsidering.

5. WHETHER AGENTS SEE ANY OF THIS. The app deliberately hides client identities from agents. Worth telling is desk-only as drawn, and that keeps the wall intact.

THE PICTURE THE CLIENT GETS -- nineteen words

You said most clients cannot read much. Everything is in English -- product names, units, the plain commercial words -- but there are almost none of them. Four frames carry FOUR PHOTOS, FIVE NUMBERS AND ABOUT NINETEEN WORDS, and every word is a label rather than a sentence.

WHAT SURVIVES LOW LITERACY, and it is the whole design: their own NAME, a PHOTO of the thing, the QUANTITY, the PRICE, and a phone NUMBER. Numbers are read by everybody who trades. So the numbers are enormous and the prose is gone.

FRAME 1 -- WHO, AND WHAT. Their name at 86px and the product photo. Two words: KATO. CEMENT.
FRAME 2 -- HOW MANY, HOW MUCH. 40 BAGS. 42,000 EACH. And one stamp -- SAME PRICE -- with a tick, in verdigris, because a price that has not moved is the single most reassuring thing you can say to somebody buying on credit. Where the price HAS moved the stamp says NEW PRICE in amber, and where it has fallen it says the old figure struck through. Never a stamp that flatters.
FRAME 3 -- ALSO NEED. Two photos, two numbers, two labels. The quantities are worked from the pairing you defined -- 0.6 kg of nails per bag -- which is what makes this frame read as a hardware man rather than an advert. No pairing with a figure means no number appears; no pairing at all means this frame is dropped and the picture is three frames.
FRAME 4 -- WHAT TO DO. REPLY YES. WE KEEP IT FOR YOU. Your number, huge, on a white pill. Three words and a phone number.

THE OLD FRAMES ARE GONE. The first draft had sentences like "Because you take 40 every 18 days, and the site is at walling." True, and useful -- to YOU. It is now on the shop's side of the screen and nowhere near the client.

EVERY CLIENT HAS ONE, which is the fifth artboard. Sarah bought once, thirty-eight days ago: six bags of cement. That is enough -- her own quantity, her own price, the same stamp. A brief built from a single order is still a brief built from THEIR dealings with you, which is the whole promise. A client with no orders at all gets three frames and no quantity: name, what the shop sells that suits their trade, and how to reach you.

WHAT GOES WITH WHAT -- the shop's own knowledge, written down

You asked for a way to describe product relationships so the algorithm can pick up from there. This is it, and it has two halves that check each other.

A PAIRING IS A SENTENCE, so it is written as one: [Iron Sheets 28 gauge] [needs] [Roofing nails] -- [8] per [sheet]. Not six form fields in a box. A hardware man says it out loud in about a second and the screen should take about as long.

FIVE VERBS, AND THEY ARE THE WHOLE VOCABULARY:
NEEDS -- it cannot be used without it. Sheets need nails. The picture says so, and this is the one that saves a return trip.
GOES WITH -- usually bought together. Offered, not insisted on.
INSTEAD OF -- a swap when the first is out of stock or too dear. Never shown unless the first is actually unavailable.
RUNS OUT AFTER -- it will be finished in about so many days, and the picture comes back round then. This is what turns a paint sale into a paint customer.
PART OF -- both belong to one job. Roofing, plumbing, finishing.

THE RATIO IS THE POINT. "8 per sheet" is what lets a picture say 140 sheets becomes 1,120 nails. Without a figure the frame still names the thing and shows its photo, and NO NUMBER APPEARS -- an invented quantity is worse than none.

THE TWO HALVES. You write pairings from what you have seen at the counter. The books find pairs that keep landing on the same invoice. Neither is trusted alone:
- YOURS, BOOKS AGREE (verdigris) -- the strongest thing this shop knows about its own goods. Used first in every picture.
- YOURS ONLY -- stands, gets used, no confirmation yet.
- BOOKS CANNOT SEE IT -- you paired cement with sand, and you do not sell sand. Still true, still useful at the counter, never in a picture.
- BOOKS ARGUE -- you wrote it, the orders do not show it. The rule STILL STANDS, because you have stood at the counter and the books have not. You are told once, here, and that is all.
- BOOKS FOUND IT -- a pair the orders keep showing, waiting on your word. Keep or No. Saying No is as useful as saying Keep: it stops being offered.

The open row shows the books checking your figure against the orders -- 47 orders with sheets, 42 with nails too, 7.6 nails per sheet on average against your 8.0. That is the shop and the ledger agreeing in public, and it is the most trustworthy thing on the screen.

A PAIRING NEVER TOUCHES PRICES, STOCK OR ORDERS. It only lets a picture say a second thing.

EVERY CLIENT HAS A BRIEF

You said it plainly: the brief should be for every client, because each one has dealings with you to build it from. So the picture is not a thing the queue produces -- it EXISTS on every customer's account, always, and the queue only decides who is worth telling this fortnight.

THE ACCOUNT CARRIES IT. Four thumbnails, a Share, and the fortnight badge. You can open anybody, look at their picture and send it by hand -- outside the queue, outside the schedule -- because sometimes you just want to.

AND UNDER IT, THE REASON, ONLY ON YOUR SIDE. "They take 40 bags every 18 days, seven times running. The site is at walling. The price has not moved since they last paid, so the picture may say same price. The third frame is your own pairing -- 0.6 kg per bag -- which your orders agree with in 11 of 14 cases."

THE SPLIT IS THE WHOLE IDEA. The client sees four photos, five numbers and nineteen words. You see the arithmetic, the evidence and what was rejected. Nothing that reads as reasoning ever reaches the picture, and nothing that reaches the picture is unexplained on your side.

The rail names what was left out and why -- binding wire was dropped because it is out of stock, and a picture never offers what the shelf cannot give.
